extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, political economy, policing, and media studies
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of policing and moral panic
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic account of the 'mugging panic' and the emergence of an 'exceptional' law-and-order state in 1970s Britain, tracing political, legal, media, and economic mechanisms that produce moral panics and authoritarian responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five essential conditions for the 'mugging panic'
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'mugging' panic depended on at least five essential conditions: (1) a state of anticipatory mobilisation and 'preparedness' in the control apparatuses; (2) a sensitising of official circles and of the public through the mass media; (3) a 'perceived danger' to social stability - such as when the crime rate is read as indexing a general break-down in social authority and control; (4) the identification of a vulnerable 'target group' (e.g. black youth) involved in dramatic incidents ('muggings') which trigger public alarm; (5) the setting in motion of the mechanisms by which conspiratorial demons and criminal folk-devils are projected on to the public stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors argue that when these five conditions are all met 'in full' the moral panic precipitates; they emphasise that the date (1972) is a focal point where multiple contradictions accumulate, but that the 'moment of mugging' has a longer inner history and must be situated within broader juridical and ideological developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interposition of the law into class relations mobilises public opinion for the 'strong state'
rubrics_metrics.description: The mobilisation of 'the law' into class relations makes it more legitimate for 'public opinion' to be actively recruited in favour of 'the strong state'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This process removes some neutral 'cover' from the law but simultaneously legitimises open, explicit recruitment of public support for repressive state measures (examples: phone-in programmes, political rhetoric). The law thus becomes a mechanism for ideological mobilisation as well as coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media legitimisation of state policy by framing matters as 'national interest'
rubrics_metrics.description: When the 'national interest' is unequivocally identified with whatever policies the state is pursuing, the media provide the raison d'être for those policies and feel legitimate in intervening on the side of the 'centre'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include press attacks on miners as 'holding the nation up to ransom', organised hounding of union leaders, reprinting of right-wing features, and systematic framing of union/internal Labour disputes in 'moderates/extremist' terms. Media intervention is portrayed as routine and legitimising rather than neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspiratorial worldview as the authorised form for explaining dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: The crisis is appropriated as an interlocking set of planned or organised conspiracies; society becomes 'fixated by the idea of a conspiracy against the British way of life' so that dissent, opposition or conflict is explained as the work of an evil minority of subversives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propagation of this conspiratorial frame makes official repression legitimate; it identifies the whole society with the state, so 'whatever the state does is legitimate (even if it is not

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the conspiracy charge as a broad engine of state policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The conspiracy charge (illustrated by the Katama decision and later prosecutions) was adapted to generalise repressive control: its terms are wide, ambiguous and designed to net whole groups of people whether complicit or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors give examples (editors charged with 'conspiracy to outrage public decency', protesters charged with conspiracy despite tenuous links) and note judicial/political framing of such decisions as 'political' law-making rather than neutral legal adjudication. Conspiracy law becomes a tool for breaking solidarity and deterring others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency and anti-terror legislation blurs policing boundaries and erodes civil liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergency legislation (e.g. anti-terror laws) and practices (e.g. Special Branch activity, arming of police) drew the police into ambiguous territory between suspicion and proof and accelerated the erosion of civil liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances like the Lennon affair, the arming trend, and the official rebukes of civil liberties organisations illustrate how legal and policing changes shift the practical limits of toleration and normalise tougher policing measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social contract as a managerial device for capitalist crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'social contract' is a form in which British social democracy attempted to preside over the effects of declining capitalism — a corporate bargain struck between the Labour government, the T.U.C., and representatives of capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early concessions aimed to 'bring about a fundamental shift in the distribution of wealth' and to give unions some formal veto; over time those commitments are whittled away via welfare cuts and constrained wages. The social contract thus functions as a fragile mechanism to secure working-class consent while enabling capitalist stabilization strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic deterioration as the material base enabling authoritarian/state 'exceptionalism'
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid deterioration of Britain's economic position (recession, high inflation, unemployment, oil shock) overdetermined the conjuncture and created conditions in which an 'exceptional' form of the capitalist state could be installed and appear permanently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links concrete policy dilemmas (freeze on wages, phased limits, miners' claims) and international credit pressures to the narrowing of political options and the transfer of crisis costs onto the working class, which in turn enables ideological and coercive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and targeting of vulnerable 'folk-devil' groups to trigger public alarm
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral panics require the identification of a vulnerable target group (for example, black youth) involved in dramatic incidents ('muggings') that trigger public alarm and focus attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process includes dramatization of incidents, projection of criminal folk-devils onto the public stage, and the racialisation or scapegoating of particular social groups as threats to social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing moral panics around apparently non-political issues to prepare ideological climate
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues presented as 'non-political' (e.g. comprehensive education, falling standards, classroom 'Reds') are used as sponsored 'moral panics' to tutor public opinion into social authoritarian postures and to prepare the terrain for political denouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: William Tyndale school controversy, press features, interventions by religious authorities; such manufactured panics make broader authoritarian measures culturally acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equating society with the state to legitimate state action
rubrics_metrics.description: When the whole of society is identified with the state — the state as the bureaucratic embodiment of the popular will — the premise becomes that 'whatever the state does is legitimate', and anyone who 'threatens the consensus threatens the state.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ideological move collapses the distinction between state and society and underwrites acceptance of repressive measures as expressions of 'popular' will rather than contested power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological assault on equality and welfare to justify tougher social discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: A coordinated swing to the right advocates elitism, dismantling of the Welfare State, and a moral backlash against 'welfare scroungers', framed as restoring self-reliance, patriotism, and traditional family values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations from political figures (e.g. Sir Keith Joseph) and campaigns (anti-abortion, Mrs Whitehouse) are cited as manifestations of an ideological project that both legitimises and accompanies coercive state measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police and judicial critique (acquittals, lenient magistrates) as a pretext for harsher measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Public criticisms by senior policing figures about high acquittal rates, 'corrupt lawyers', and lenient magistrates are used rhetorically to argue for changes that would enable tougher policing and less reliance on jury verdicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites appeals to the press and policy recommendations (e.g. James Committee) as instances where policing discourse is marshalled to justify legal and procedural tightening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to situate reactions within shifting balance between different state apparatuses and long historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: The reaction to 'mugging' can only be understood via the shifting balance and internal relations between different state apparatuses (police, courts, media) in relation to the management of crisis; the 'mugging' moment has an 'inner history' and long antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors warn against forcing neat causal fits and stress the need to reconstruct the internal histories of apparatuses and to consider the wider capitalist/global recession context when explaining the emergence and form of moral panics and state responses.
